summary.text: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all forms of life, built from a semipermeable membrane around cytoplasm that holds genetic material.
Every organism is either a prokaryote, which lacks a membrane-bound nucleus, or a eukaryote, whose nucleus is enclosed in a nuclear membrane.
Eukaryotic cells also contain other membrane-bound organelles, such as mitochondria, which provide energy for cell functions.

facts.label: Cell theory
facts.value: Developed by Schleiden in 1838 and Schwann in 1839

items.prompt: A microbiologist studies a single-celled organism whose DNA sits in a region of the cytoplasm with no membrane around it. What kind of organism is it?

options.label: A eukaryote, since eukaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleoid
A prokaryote, since it has a nucleoid instead of a nucleus
A somatic cell, since it carries a full set of chromosomes
A gamete, since single cells keep their DNA unenclosed

items.explain: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and have a nucleoid, where the DNA touches the cytoplasm directly.

items.prompt: A student claims a living cell can appear out of nothing, with no earlier cell involved. Which idea from cell theory does this break?

options.label: Every organism must be built from many cells at once
Every cell must contain a membrane-bound nucleus
Every cell must be big enough to see unaided
Every cell comes from a cell that already existed

items.explain: Cell theory states that all cells come from pre-existing cells.

items.prompt: A drug blocks the part of a eukaryotic cell that provides energy for cell functions. Which structure is affected?

options.label: The nuclear membrane, which encloses the nucleus
Ribosomes, which are organelles without a membrane
Mitochondria, the membrane-bound organelles that supply energy
The nucleoid, the region that holds the DNA

items.explain: Mitochondria are the membrane-bound organelles that provide energy for cell functions.

items.prompt: Mycoplasma has only a cell membrane, so it lacks which protective layer that most bacteria have outside their membrane?

options.label: A nucleoid that holds its DNA
A cell wall of peptidoglycan
A set of ribosomes in the cytoplasm
A circular chromosome in the cytoplasm

items.explain: Most bacteria have a cell wall of peptidoglycan outside the membrane; Mycoplasma only possesses the cell membrane.

items.prompt: Someone says every bacterium is too small to see without a microscope. What is a fair reply?

options.label: That is right, because no bacterium exceeds 5.0 micrometres
That is wrong, because every bacterium forms a visible many-celled body
That is wrong, because only yeasts are too small to see
One known species, Thiomargarita magnifica, averages 1 cm and is visible unaided

items.explain: Most prokaryotes are tiny, but Thiomargarita magnifica averages about 1 cm and can be seen with the naked eye.

paragraphs.heading: The unit of life
paragraphs.text: A cell is the basic unit of structure and function in every living thing. The name comes from the Latin cellula, a small room. At its simplest, a cell is a membrane that lets some things through, wrapped around the cytoplasm, which holds the genetic material. Most cells can only be seen through a microscope. Apart from highly specialised kinds, such as red blood cells and gametes, most can copy themselves and make proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Two big groups
paragraphs.text: All living things are sorted into two groups. Prokaryotes, which include bacteria and archaea, are always single cells and have no nucleus wrapped in membrane; their DNA sits in a region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes can be single cells or many-celled, and keep their nucleus inside a nuclear membrane. Animals, plants, most fungi and some algae are eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: Compartments inside
paragraphs.text: Eukaryotic cells also hold other compartments wrapped in membrane, called organelles. Mitochondria supply energy for the cell's work, and chloroplasts in plants make sugars through photosynthesis. Some organelles have no membrane at all, such as ribosomes, which both groups have in somewhat different forms. Prokaryotic cells are smaller and simpler, and lack a nucleus and the other membrane-bound organelles usually present in eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: A bacterium's coat
paragraphs.text: A bacterium is enclosed in a protective cell envelope. Usually this is a plasma membrane covered by a cell wall, and some bacteria add a gel-like capsule on top. The envelope gives the cell its stiffness and screens it from its surroundings. The wall, made of peptidoglycan, also keeps the cell from swelling and bursting from osmotic pressure when its surroundings are hypotonic. Inside, the DNA is usually a single circular chromosome lying in direct contact with the cytoplasm, in the nucleoid.

paragraphs.heading: From specks to centimetres
paragraphs.text: Most prokaryotes are the smallest organisms of all, between 0.1 and 5.0 μm across. Yet the largest known bacterium, Thiomargarita magnifica, can be seen with the naked eye. It averages 1 cm long and can reach 2 cm.

paragraphs.heading: How cells were found
paragraphs.text: Cells appeared on Earth around four billion years ago. Robert Hooke found them in 1665 and named them for their likeness to the cells of a monastery. In 1838 and 1839, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann showed that plants and animals are built from cells as their basic structural unit. Their cell theory holds that every organism is made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and that each cell comes from an earlier cell.
